neighbours.label: ' can' (more weakly ' as', ' to') at the point where expository text states what a thing is able to do or is used for ('They can be used to…', 'because it can…'), not personal ability or permission
fire: Logarithms matter in acoustics. They can be used to compare very different sound levels.
Vitamin K is essential because it can activate the proteins that clot blood.
Tensors are common in mechanics. They can describe stress in every direction at once.
Wetlands are valuable because they can absorb floodwater and filter pollutants.
Graphs are basic tools in computing. They can be used to model networks and schedules.
Antibodies are useful in diagnosis because they can bind to a single target molecule.
Capacitors appear in most circuits. They can store charge and release it quickly.
Mangroves protect coasts because they can break the force of incoming waves.
quiet: My cousins live near the stadium. They can come to the match on Sunday.
Vitamin K was discovered in 1929 by a Danish scientist studying chickens.
The twins are free on Friday. They can pick you up after work.
Wetlands covered much of the county before the railway was built.
Ask the neighbours first. They can say no if they are busy.
Antibodies were first described in the 1890s by researchers in Berlin.
The kids finished their homework. They can watch a film now.
Mangroves grow along tropical coasts in salty, muddy water.

notes: Card: ' can' x6, ' to' x4, ' as' x4 in statements of capability or purpose; the - pole fires on 'why do I need this / relevance / useful', so the neuron seems to separate stating a function from asking about usefulness. Weak pole (max 7.25, 43% echo regime). Probes: 'They can be used to' 0.33, 'they can break down' 0.27, 'as a way of' 0.26, 'it can move glucose' 0.22; 'ability of the eye to' 0.08, 'They can meet us' 0.03, 'She can not come' 0.03.
